title: WordPress Custom Themes vs Page Builders: What 4 Years of Agency Work Taught Me
metaTitle: WordPress Custom Themes vs Page Builders
metaDescription: A WordPress developer's honest breakdown of when to use Elementor or Divi versus a custom ACF theme, with real cost and timeline ranges.
keywords: WordPress page builder vs custom theme
excerpt: Page builders get a site live faster and cheaper; custom ACF themes cost more and take longer but pay off in speed and long-term flexibility. Here's how I actually decide between them.

content.text: Page builders like Elementor and Divi get a project live faster and cost less upfront; custom WordPress themes built with ACF cost more and take longer, but pay off in load speed, long-term maintainability, and how easily a site can grow. Here's how I actually decide between them on client work.
What's actually different between a page builder and a custom theme?

Page builders like Elementor Pro and Divi generate their own markup and CSS on top of WordPress, and give you a visual, drag-and-drop editor. A custom theme built with Advanced Custom Fields (ACF) has hand-written templates and only ships the CSS and JS the site actually needs — nothing extra just because the builder might need it for some other page.
When a page builder is the right call

items: Budget is tight and the site needs to launch fast — a builder gets simple sites live in days, not weeks
The client (or their team) wants to edit pages themselves after launch, without touching code
The site is mostly static marketing pages without complex custom functionality
It's a landing page or temporary homepage that's likely to be redesigned again soon anyway

content.text: When a custom ACF theme is worth the extra cost

items: Page speed and Core Web Vitals matter — no page builder ships as little code as a hand-built theme
The site needs custom content structures (flexible content blocks, repeaters) that a generic builder handles awkwardly
It's a WooCommerce store or has other complex functionality where builder overhead compounds
The client plans to keep and grow the site for years, not months

content.text: Page builder vs. custom theme, side by side

rows: Higher — only ships what the site needs
Small sites, self-editing clients, quick launches
WooCommerce stores, custom content needs, long-term sites

content.text: What I actually recommend to clients

I don't default to one or the other — I ask about budget, timeline, and how long the client plans to keep the site before recommending a page builder build or a custom ACF theme. Most of my work spans both: Elementor Pro and Divi when speed or budget calls for it, fully custom themes when performance or long-term flexibility matters more. If you're not sure which fits your project, that's the first thing I sort out on a call.

title: How Much Does a WordPress Developer Cost in the Philippines? (2026 Rates)

excerpt: Real rate ranges for hiring a WordPress developer in the Philippines in 2026 — hourly, retainer, and per-project — broken down by whether you're a local business or hiring internationally.

content.text: "How much does a WordPress developer cost?" is one of the first questions I get from prospective clients, and the honest answer is: it depends on where you're based, how you're hiring, and what you need built. Below are the actual rate ranges I quote in 2026, broken out by engagement type, so you can budget before we even get on a call.
Hourly rates
International direct clients pay more per hour than platform-sourced work, mainly because platform fees and client acquisition risk get priced in on marketplaces like Upwork.
Per-project rates

rows: Custom theme with ACF flexible content

content.text: Monthly retainer rates

items: Part-time (20 hrs/week), international: $1,200–2,400/month (~₱68k–135k)
Part-time, PH-based company: ₱25k–45k/month
Maintenance / support retainer, per site: $150–400/month

content.text: What actually moves the price

items: Custom ACF theme vs. page builder — custom code costs more upfront but ships less bloat long-term
WooCommerce or other complex functionality vs. a static business site
Whether you're hiring locally in the Philippines, hiring an international freelancer direct, or sourcing through a platform
One-off project vs. ongoing retainer — retainers are priced for predictable monthly work, not per-task

content.text: My honest take

If a quote for a standard WordPress business site comes in well under $600 or ₱25,000, ask what's being cut — usually it's either a page builder stretched past what it's good at, or no real testing or SEO setup before launch. On the other end, a five-figure quote for a simple brochure site is a sign you're paying for agency overhead rather than the actual build. These ranges reflect what real projects in my portfolio cost, not a rate card built to look competitive.

title: How to Update WordPress Safely: A Developer's Plugin, PHP & Core Checklist
metaTitle: How to Update WordPress Safely: Plugin, PHP & Core Checklist
metaDescription: A WordPress developer's real pre-update checklist for plugins, PHP, and core — what to read first, where to track update news, and the red flags that mean wait.
keywords: when to update PHP version WordPress
excerpt: Updating WordPress isn't just clicking "Update Now." Here's the pre-update checklist I actually run before touching plugins, PHP, or core on a live client site — and where I get the news that tells me when to wait.

content.text: Most site-breaking WordPress issues I get called in to fix didn't come from a hack — they came from an update. A plugin update that dropped support for an old PHP version, a core update that exposed an incompatible plugin, a PHP bump that silently broke a theme function. None of this is random; it's what happens when updates get clicked without reading anything first. Here's the actual checklist I run.
Read before you update — every time

items: The plugin's changelog for that specific version — not just "bug fixes," look for the words "breaking," "deprecated," "removed," or "requires"
"Tested up to" WordPress version and "Requires PHP" version on the plugin's page — if your site is ahead of both, that's a signal, not a guarantee
The plugin's support forum or GitHub issues, filtered to the last 7–14 days, for anyone reporting the new version broke something
Whether the version number jumped a major digit (2.x to 3.x) — that's the industry convention for "expect breaking changes," even if the changelog undersells it

content.text: Where I actually get update news

items: WordPress.org News (wordpress.org/news) for core release announcements and security releases
The plugin's own changelog tab on wordpress.org, not the marketing copy on its homepage
Patchstack and WPScan's vulnerability databases — catches security-driven updates before they hit mainstream news
PHP.net's supported-versions page, so I know a PHP version's active support and end-of-life dates before a host forces a bump
The plugin author's own blog or X/Twitter account, for major plugins where breaking changes get announced ahead of release

content.text: The update order that avoids most disasters

items: Full backup — files and database — before touching anything, confirmed restorable, not just "a backup exists somewhere"
Test the update on a staging copy first, especially for core, PHP, or any plugin handling payments, forms, or custom fields
Update plugins one at a time, not in bulk — bulk updates make it much harder to tell which plugin broke something if the site breaks
Update PHP version separately from plugin/core updates, and only after checking every active plugin's declared PHP compatibility
Update core last, after confirming the active theme and plugins are already fine on the new PHP version

content.text: Red flags that mean wait, don't update yet

items: The plugin hasn't been updated in 12+ months and is only tested up to an old WordPress version — a forced update later will be worse, but rushing now isn't the fix either
The new version dropped within the last few days and support threads are already reporting issues
A PHP version bump with no compatibility statement from a business-critical plugin (payments, booking, membership)
You don't have a tested, restorable backup — this alone should stop any update on a live site

content.text: Safe to update now vs. test on staging first

rows: Security patch, no version jump, active support threads are quiet
Major version bump (breaking changes flagged in changelog)
PHP version bump on a site with payment or booking plugins
Staging first, check every plugin's PHP compatibility
Plugin update on a site with no recent backup

content.text: What this looks like on a maintenance retainer

This is exactly what I run on client maintenance retainers — reading changelogs, checking PHP compatibility, staging-testing anything that touches core or payments, and only then pushing to production. It's slower than clicking "Update Now" on everything at once, but it's the difference between a maintenance retainer and an emergency fix call.

title: SEO Rates & Packages in the Philippines (2026): What You Actually Pay For
metaTitle: SEO Rates & Packages Philippines (2026): Real Prices
metaDescription: SEO pricing in the Philippines for 2026: audit, speed optimization and monthly SEO package rates in pesos and dollars, plus what each one actually includes.
keywords: SEO rates and packages in the Philippines
how much does SEO cost Philippines
excerpt: Real 2026 SEO rates in the Philippines: what a technical SEO audit, page speed work, and a monthly SEO package cost, and how to tell a fair quote from one that will waste your budget.

content.text: SEO in the Philippines costs anywhere from a few thousand pesos to six figures a month, and the price alone tells you very little. Below are the rates I quote in 2026 as a Metro Manila-based SEO specialist, broken down by package, plus what each one includes so you can compare quotes on what's actually delivered.
SEO rates in the Philippines at a glance

rows: Sites that aren't showing up in Google and nobody knows why
Slow sites, failing Core Web Vitals in Search Console
Ongoing SEO, billed hourly (local PH clients)
Monthly fixes, monitoring, and on-page updates

content.text: What's in a technical SEO audit

items: Crawl the whole site with Screaming Frog to find broken links, redirect chains, duplicate titles, and pages Google can't reach
Review Google Search Console: which pages are indexed, which are excluded, and why
Check titles, meta descriptions, and heading structure against what people actually search for
Add or fix structured data (schema) so Google understands the business, services, and FAQs
Fix the issues found, not just hand over a PDF. The implementation is part of the price

content.text: What a monthly SEO package should include

Most Philippine small businesses don't need a big monthly agency retainer. They need a few hours each month of someone checking Search Console, fixing what broke, and improving the pages that are close to ranking. At ₱500–900/hr, 10 hours a month comes to roughly ₱5,000–9,000. That time typically covers:

items: Monthly Search Console review: new errors, pages dropping out of the index, queries gaining impressions
Rewriting titles and descriptions on pages that get impressions but no clicks
Internal linking from new content to the pages you want to rank
Keeping plugins, schema, and sitemaps working after site updates
A short report in plain language: what changed, what improved, what's next

content.text: Red flags in cheap SEO packages

items: Guaranteed page-one rankings. Nobody controls Google's results, and anyone who promises this is guessing or lying
"500 backlinks a month" for a few thousand pesos. Bulk links from spam sites can get you penalized
No access to your own Search Console or Analytics. You should own your data
Reports full of vanity numbers but no list of what was actually changed on your site

content.text: How long until SEO shows results?

Technical fixes like speed and indexing problems usually show up in Search Console within a few weeks. Ranking for competitive keywords takes months, especially for a new site. A healthy early sign is impressions climbing even before clicks do: it means Google is testing your pages for those searches.
Where to start

If you're not sure what your site needs, start with a technical SEO audit. You'll get a clear list of what's holding the site back and what it costs to fix, before committing to anything monthly. See my SEO services page for the full scope, or the pricing page for every rate in one place.
